title: The Tide That Kept Score
summary: On the shore of Gullstrand, the tide gives back whatever you give it — a kindness returns doubled, a cruelty returns doubled too. When Bram uses the tide to take revenge on the boy who wronged him, he learns that a sea that keeps score will keep his, and has to find a way to stop a wave he set in motion.

chapters.title: What the Tide Returns
chapters.body:
The shore of Gullstrand had a strange and ancient rule, and the fisherfolk who lived there had built their whole way of life around it: the tide gave back whatever you gave it.

Not the same thing — more than the same thing. If you cast bread upon the water for the hungry gulls, the tide would return you a net heavy with fish. If you saved a stranded seal pup and carried it back to the waves, the sea would carry your boat safely through the next storm. Kindness given to the tide came back doubled, tripled, a rising flood of good fortune. The people of Gullstrand were, by and large, the most generous folk on the coast — not because they were saints, but because they had learned, over generations, that generosity paid. The tide kept score, and it always, always settled its accounts.

But the rule ran both ways. And that was the part the fisherfolk taught their children early and gravely. If you gave the tide cruelty — if you fouled the water out of spite, if you took more than you needed and wasted the rest, if you drowned a thing for the pleasure of it — that came back doubled too. A rising flood of misfortune. The tide did not judge, did not forgive, did not distinguish between a kindness and a cruelty. It only gave back what it was given, multiplied, without mercy. And so the one true law of Gullstrand was: be careful what you give the sea, because the sea will give it back to you, and more.

Bram was thirteen, and he had been wronged, and he wanted the tide to help him settle it.

The boy who'd wronged him was named Coll — a bigger boy, a cruel one, who had spent the summer making Bram's life miserable. Coll had wrecked Bram's fishing lines, and shoved him in the mud in front of the others, and, worst of all, had smashed the little carved boat that Bram's late father had made him, the last thing Bram had of him, splintering it against the rocks and laughing. Bram had wept over the pieces. And the weeping had turned, over the long summer, into a hard hot knot of anger, and the anger had turned into a plan.

Bram knew the rule of the tide. And he thought: if the sea gives back what I give it — then I will give it my hatred. I will give it a curse against Coll, cast upon the water, and the tide will return it doubled, and Coll will drown in the misfortune of it, and it will serve him right.

So one grey dawn, Bram went down to the water alone, and he waded in to his knees, and he did the forbidden thing. He gave the tide his cruelty. He cast his hatred of Coll upon the waves — spoke it aloud, all of it, every wish for harm — and asked the sea to carry it to Coll and give it back doubled. To wreck Coll's boat as Coll had wrecked his. To shame him. To hurt him. To make him suffer.

The grey water took the words, and swirled around Bram's knees, and drew back out to sea carrying his curse. And Bram walked home with the hard hot knot in his chest feeling, for the first time all summer, something like satisfaction.

He did not yet understand what he had done.

chapters.title: The Wave He Set in Motion
chapters.body:
The tide returned Bram's cruelty three days later, and it was worse than he had imagined — and not at all the way he'd planned.

It began with Coll, just as Bram had asked. A freak wave swamped Coll's family's boat at its mooring and sank it, and the nets were fouled and torn, and Coll's father — who had done nothing to anyone — lost the season's catch and wept at the ruin of it. Bram, watching from the shore, felt a flash of the satisfaction he'd wanted. It had worked. The tide had given his cruelty back to Coll, doubled.

But the tide, Bram was about to learn, does not aim. It does not understand who deserves what. It only gives back what it was given, multiplied, and lets the flood spread where it will. And a doubled cruelty is a great deal of misfortune to loose upon a small village.

The bad luck did not stop with Coll. It spread. The fouled water sickened the fish in the shallows, and other families' catches failed too. The freak waves that had sunk Coll's boat kept coming, and battered the harbor wall, and a fishing family Bram had known all his life lost their boat as well — a kind old couple who had never wronged anyone. The misfortune Bram had loosed rolled through Gullstrand like a rising flood, exactly as the rule promised, touching the guilty and the innocent alike, because the tide kept score without conscience and settled its accounts without care for who stood in the way.

And it got worse, because misfortune, once loosed, breeds more. A hungry, frightened village grows angry. Neighbors who lost their catches began to blame one another. Old friends quarreled. Coll's father, ruined and desperate, lashed out at another man, and the two came to blows, and the hard feeling spread further, and the whole warm generous village that had been built on kindness given to the sea began to curdle into something bitter and frightened and cruel.

And here was the horror Bram had not foreseen. In a village where the tide gives back what it's given, a spreading cruelty is a catastrophe — because now the frightened, angry villagers, without even meaning to, were giving their own bitterness to the sea. Their quarrels, their spite, their desperation, all of it washing into the water day by day. And the tide was taking it, and doubling it, and giving it back. The misfortune was feeding itself. Bram had cast one stone of hatred into the water, and it had started a wave, and the wave was building on itself, cruelty breeding cruelty breeding cruelty, and it would not stop on its own. It would roll on, doubling and doubling, until it drowned the whole village that Bram loved.

Bram stood on the shore and watched what he had done spreading out of all control, and the hard hot knot of anger in his chest turned, at last, into something else: horror, and shame, and a desperate need to undo it. He had wanted to hurt one cruel boy. He had set in motion something that would destroy them all.

He had to stop the wave. But you cannot un-cast a thing upon the water. The tide had his cruelty now, and it would keep giving it back, doubled, forever — unless Bram could find something stronger to give it instead.

chapters.title: The Only Thing Stronger
chapters.body:
Bram went to the oldest fisherwoman in Gullstrand, a woman so old she was said to remember the tide's rule from the inside, and he confessed everything — the curse he'd cast, the wave he'd started, the flood of misfortune spreading through the village. He begged her to tell him how to stop it.

The old woman listened, and her face was grave, and when Bram had finished she was quiet for a long, frightening moment.

"You've done a terrible thing," she said at last. "Not because you were angry — anger is human, and that boy wronged you badly. But because you gave your anger to the sea. And the sea cannot un-take a gift. Your cruelty is in the water now, and it will keep coming back, doubled, and every doubling stirs more cruelty in the village, which feeds the water more, which comes back worse. That is the wave you started. And no, child — you cannot un-cast it. What's given to the tide is given."

"Then it can't be stopped," Bram whispered, despairing. "I've drowned us all."

"I didn't say that." The old woman fixed him with her ancient eyes. "The tide gives back what it's given, multiplied. You gave it cruelty, and cruelty is flooding back. You cannot take that cruelty out of the water. But you can give the water something else. Something stronger. And there is only one thing stronger than a doubled cruelty — and that is a greater kindness, given freely, and given again, and again, until it outweighs the cruelty and turns the tide." She leaned close. "But hear me. It will not be easy, and it will not be quick, and it will not be fair. You'll have to give the sea more kindness than you gave it cruelty — far more, because you have a doubling flood to overcome. And here is the hardest part, child: the first and greatest kindness you must give is to the one person you least want to help. You must give your kindness to Coll."

Bram recoiled. "Coll? He's the one who — he smashed my father's boat! He started all of this! Why should I —"

"Because that," said the old woman, "is where the cruelty began, and that is where the kindness must begin, if it's to be stronger. Anyone can be kind to a friend. To give the sea a kindness strong enough to turn a flood of hate, you must do the hardest thing there is: be kind to the one who wronged you. Not because he deserves it. Because it's the only thing strong enough."

And Bram understood, then, the terrible and beautiful shape of what he had to do. He could not undo his revenge. But he could outweigh it — with a harder, greater, freely given kindness, starting with the boy he hated most.

So Bram began. It was the hardest thing he had ever done. Coll's family had lost their boat to the very wave Bram had cast — so Bram went to them, and said nothing of his guilt, and simply helped. He gave them fish from his own lines. He worked beside Coll's weeping father to mend the fouled nets. He waded into the water each dawn and gave the tide a kindness — real kindness, freely given, no longer a curse but a gift: help for the hungry, care for the village, and, hardest of all, forgiveness for Coll. He gave it and gave it, day after day, and it cost him more than the revenge ever had, because the revenge had been easy and hot and this was hard and cold and slow.

And at first, nothing changed. The flood of misfortune rolled on. But Bram kept giving, and slowly — so slowly he almost didn't believe it — the tide began to turn. The kindness he cast upon the water came back, doubled, just as the rule promised: a good catch here, a mended quarrel there, a family's luck turning. And the returning kindness stirred kindness in the village, the way the cruelty had stirred cruelty — neighbors helping neighbors now, the bitter feeling thawing, the villagers giving their own restored goodwill back to the sea, which doubled it, which came back better. The wave was turning. Kindness was breeding kindness now, exactly as cruelty had bred cruelty, and the flood that had nearly drowned Gullstrand began, at last, to recede.

And the strangest thing of all: somewhere in those long hard days of forced kindness, Bram's hatred of Coll quietly died. He had set out to be kind to Coll as a kind of medicine, gritting his teeth through it. But you cannot help mend a weeping man's nets, and share your fish with his hungry family, and work beside his son day after day, without the hate wearing away. By the time the tide had fully turned, Bram found he no longer hated Coll at all. And Coll — humbled by the ruin, and confused and then ashamed by the kindness of the boy he'd tormented — came to Bram one day, red-faced, and mumbled an apology, and offered, awkwardly, to help Bram carve a new boat to replace the one he'd smashed. And they carved it together. It was not as fine as the one Bram's father had made. But it was made in friendship, out of the wreckage of a hatred, and Bram loved it for that.

Gullstrand healed. The tide ran gentle and generous again, because the village gave it kindness again, and the terrible summer became a story the old ones told the children as a warning.

And the warning was this: the sea keeps score, and so does the world, and what you give it comes back to you, doubled, whether you meant it or not. A cruelty cast upon the water does not stay where you aim it — it spreads, and doubles, and drowns the innocent along with the guilty, and comes back to you worst of all. But a kindness does the same. And so the only wise way to live, on the shore of Gullstrand or anywhere else, is to be very, very careful what you give the tide — because the tide is always rising, and it always, always brings back what you gave.
